title: 2003 AMC 12B 18
statement: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be positive integers such that \(7x^5 = 11y^{13}.\) The minimum possible value of \(x\) has a prime factorization \(a^c b^d.\) What is \(a + b + c + d?\)

solutions.text:
For the minimum \(x,\) neither \(x\) nor \(y\) has prime factors other than \(7\) and \(11.\) Write \(x = 7^c 11^d,\) so \(7x^5 = 7^{5c+1} 11^{5d}.\) Writing \(y = 7^m 11^n,\) we need \(7^{5c+1}11^{5d} = 7^{13m}11^{13n+1}.\)

Matching exponents: \(5c + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{13}\) gives the least \(c = 5,\) and \(5d \equiv 1 \pmod{13}\) gives the least \(d = 8.\) So \(a = 7,\) \(b = 11,\) and \[ \begin{aligned} &a + b + c + d \\ &= 7 + 11 + 5 + 8 = 31. \end{aligned} \]

Thus, the correct answer is B.
hints: The minimum \(x\) uses only the primes \(7\) and \(11,\) so write \(x = 7^c 11^d\)
Match exponents of \(7\) and \(11:\) need \(5c + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{13}\) and \(5d \equiv 1 \pmod{13}\)
